solutions.explanation:
Let \(g(t)=|t|-1\) and \(T=f_0(x)\). We need the value obtained after \(100\) applications of \(g\) to be \(0\). The useful observation is that positive integers decrease by \(1\), while \(0\) and \(-1\) alternate.

An integer output of \(g\) can only come from an integer input: if \(|t|-1\) is an integer, then \(|t|\), and hence \(t\), is an integer. Working backward from the final \(0\), we see that \(T\) must be an integer.

Set \(a=|T|\). If \(a>0\), the first output is \(a-1\), and the values then decrease by \(1\) until reaching \(0\) after \(a\) applications. If \(a>100\), the value after \(100\) applications is still positive. Once \(0\) is reached, the cycle is
\[
0\longmapsto-1\longmapsto0.
\]
This also covers \(a=0\), where the starting value is already \(0\). Thus the final value is \(0\) exactly when \(a\le100\) and \(100-a\) is even. Equivalently,
\[
T\in\{-100,-98,\ldots,98,100\}.
\]
Now simplify the initial function on disjoint intervals:
\[
f_0(x)=
\begin{cases}
x+200,&x<-100,\\
-x,&-100\le x\le100,\\
x-200,&x>100.
\end{cases}
\]
For each target \(-100<T<100\), its three solutions are \(x=T-200,-T,T+200\), one in each branch. There are \(99\) such even targets. At \(T=-100\), the distinct solutions are \(-300,100\); at \(T=100\), they are \(-100,300\). The branch endpoints have been counted only once.

Therefore the number of values of \(x\) is
\[
99\cdot3+2\cdot2=\boxed{301},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
solutions.title: Follow the descent and the two-step cycle

solutions.explanation:
Let \(g(t)=|t|-1\), and let \(S_j\) be the set of starting values whose output is \(0\) after \(j\) applications of \(g\). Starting with \(S_0=\{0\}\), we can find each preceding set by solving \(|t|-1=u\).

A target \(u<-1\) has no predecessor. For \(u\ge-1\), its predecessors are \(t=\pm(u+1)\), with just one value, \(0\), when \(u=-1\). This gives
\[
S_1=\{-1,1\},\qquad S_2=\{-2,0,2\}.
\]
The general pattern is
\[
S_j=\{-j,-j+2,\ldots,j-2,j\}.
\]
Here is why the pattern continues. If \(j\) is even, the usable targets in this set are \(0,2,\ldots,j\); their predecessors are exactly \(\pm1,\pm3,\ldots,\pm(j+1)\). If \(j\) is odd, the usable targets are \(-1,1,3,\ldots,j\); their predecessors are exactly \(0,\pm2,\ldots,\pm(j+1)\). Starting from \(S_0\), these two transitions prove the pattern for every \(j\), including all possible predecessors.

Thus \(f_{100}(x)=0\) exactly when \(f_0(x)\) is one of the \(101\) even integers from \(-100\) to \(100\).

The initial function is
\[
f_0(x)=
\begin{cases}
x+200,&x<-100,\\
-x,&-100\le x\le100,\\
x-200,&x>100.
\end{cases}
\]
Each branch is one-to-one. The left branch has range \(( -\infty,100)\), so it reaches \(100\) of the target values, excluding only \(100\). The middle branch reaches all \(101\) targets. The right branch has range \((-100,\infty)\), so it reaches \(100\) targets, excluding only \(-100\). These input branches are disjoint, so their counts add without duplication.

The total is \(100+101+100=\boxed{301}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
